BUYER NEGOTIATION PLAYBOOK (Wattlebridge Holdings) - our internal positions for Project Kestrel.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

## Executive view

The Seller’s package departs materially from our playbook. Its principal strategy is to place virtually every claim—including title and potentially fraud, indemnity, tax, IP and covenant claims—inside a low-cap, short-period general warranty regime, while using broad deemed disclosure and Buyer-knowledge exclusions to reduce that regime further.

We should not accept the draft as a package. In particular, no authority has been given by Amelia Frost to accept either the 20% general cap or the 18-month claim period.

## Principal departures and required pushback

| Issue | Seller position | Required Buyer position and reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| **General warranty cap** | 20% / AUD 4.8m | Reinstate **25% / AUD 6m**. The 20% position is only an authorised fallback with Amelia Frost’s prior written approval identifying the draft; no such approval exists. |
| **De minimis and basket** | AUD 25,000 per claim; AUD 250,000 basket; only excess recoverable | Reinstate **AUD 5,000 de minimis and AUD 50,000 tipping basket**, with Seller liable from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded. Seller’s proposal materially suppresses legitimate claims and converts the basket into a deductible. Appropriate aggregation of related claims should be permitted. |
| **General claim period** | 18 months | Reinstate **24 months after Completion**. Eighteen months requires Amelia Frost’s prior written approval, which has not been given. Notice given within the period must preserve the claim. |
| **Title and fundamental warranties** | Same cap and time limit as general warranties | Reject. Title, ownership, authority and capacity need a **separate regime**, a **100% purchase-price cap**, at least **six years**, and exclusion from the general basket, de minimis and Buyer-knowledge bar. A defective share title cannot sensibly be treated as an ordinary operational warranty claim capped at 20%. |
| **“All Claims” limitation override** | Limitations apply to all Claims unless expressly excluded | Reject and redraft by claim category. General warranties, title/fundamental claims, tax, IP, specific indemnities, payment obligations and covenants must remain separate. Avoid definitions or priority clauses that silently apply the general cap, time bar or thresholds across the agreement. |
| **Fraud and misconduct** | Caps, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to all claims “of any nature” | Insert an express, overriding carve-out for **fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct**, to the maximum extent enforceable, from every cap, threshold, time limit, exclusive-remedy provision and non-reliance clause. This is non-negotiable under the playbook. The carve-out should prevail over inconsistent provisions. |
| **General disclosure** | Entire data room, accounts, registers and public searches deemed disclosed | Reject. Only matters **specifically and fairly disclosed**, with sufficient detail to identify the nature and reasonably assess the scope and consequences of the matter, should qualify warranties. Delete whole-data-room, public-register and prudent-search/deemed-discovery concepts. |
| **Buyer knowledge** | No claim for anything Buyer or advisers knew or could discover from the data room or public records | Delete the blanket exclusion. It improperly turns constructive knowledge and adviser knowledge into a broad defence and undermines negotiated warranties. In no event may knowledge qualify title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity. Any knowledge-qualified Seller warranty should use named Seller knowledge persons and reasonable enquiry. |
| **Exclusive remedies/non-reliance** | Apply to all claims | Limit carefully and preserve the separate claim regimes, contractual debt/payment claims, specific indemnities and enforcement of covenants. Expressly carve out fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct. Non-reliance must not neutralise express warranties or disclosures required to be accurate. |

## Transaction-specific matters

### 1. Bluefen consent — material Completion condition

Bluefen represents approximately AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue, or roughly 30%. The Disclosure Letter confirms that neither final consent nor evidence of satisfaction of its conditions is available.

We should require, before Completion:

- effective written change-control consent in an agreed form;
- evidence that all conditions in clause 11.3 have been satisfied or validly waived;
- confirmation that the consent remains effective and has not been withdrawn or adversely qualified; and
- no material amendment, concession or value leakage given to secure it without Buyer approval.

“Reasonable endeavours” and deeming the condition satisfied merely upon delivery of a document are inadequate for a customer of this significance. If this is not achieved, the Buyer should retain the right not to complete; it should not become merely a post-Completion claim.

### 2. Riverlark facility and security

The facility remains approximately AUD 3.2m outstanding, and no final security discharge is included. A release “following Completion” exposes the Buyer to acquiring shares in a company still subject to third-party debt and security.

Require:

- a current lender payout letter;
- an agreed funds-flow item paying Riverlark directly from Completion proceeds;
- effective releases and discharges of all guarantees, security interests and related claims at Completion;
- evidence enabling prompt PPSR and other relevant release registrations; and
- confirmation that no further amounts are outstanding.

A post-Completion release is not acceptable absent an irrevocable lender undertaking and Amelia Frost’s specific approval.

### 3. Completion bonuses and on-costs

The AUD 420,000 DD-005 bonuses are triggered by Completion but omitted from the funds flow. They cannot remain an unallocated Company liability in a debt-free/cash-free acquisition.

Require:

- a separate funds-flow line item;
- Seller funding or an express purchase-price/debt-like adjustment;
- calculation and allocation of payroll tax, superannuation and any other on-costs;
- confirmation of who pays, when payment occurs and whether all related liabilities are discharged; and
- protection against double counting under any other adjustment mechanism.

The Seller’s statement that the bonuses are “a matter for the Seller” is insufficient unless the documents and funds flow make that outcome legally and mechanically effective.

### 4. Ironquay IP

The present indemnity is too narrow if it only covers the specific SOW3 payment. DD-004 suggests ownership transfer depends on payment of all SOW3 fees, while DD-010’s AUD 180,000 entry is not independent evidence of the actual balance or payment status.

Require:

- an up-to-date statement from Ironquay confirming all amounts due;
- direct payment or other agreed cure at Completion;
- written confirmation/assignment establishing that the Company owns the relevant Project Materials;
- evidence that Ironquay retains no lien, encumbrance or ownership claim; and
- a broader specific indemnity covering unpaid fees, failure of assignment/ownership, related third-party claims, remediation costs and loss arising from the historic Ironquay arrangements.

The agreed SOW3 cure should be preserved. We should not affirmatively accept or reject AUD 180,000 as the verified liability until independent confirmation is received.

### 5. Export/privacy incident

The Disclosure Letter appropriately does **not** establish access by an unauthorised person, the exact affected population, a reportable breach, loss or a notification obligation. We should not allow the Seller to minimise it as immaterial, but equally should not assume an established breach or impose an unsupported numeric adjustment.

Require:

- preservation of relevant logs, mail records and forensic evidence;
- a properly scoped investigation;
- regular updates and immediate notice of material developments;
- Buyer consultation before notifications, admissions, regulator engagement or remediation, subject to legal requirements;
- delivery of the final investigation report and supporting evidence; and
- appropriate warranty/covenant protection for the accuracy and completeness of information supplied.

The disclosure should be confined to the facts specifically stated and should not operate as a blanket exception for all privacy, security or regulatory consequences.

### 6. Sandbar renewals

The three AUD 110,000 renewals should not automatically be treated as Debt or deducted from price. But the Seller’s assertion that they are ordinary-course costs is not established by the disclosure.

Investigate:

- execution and renewal dates;
- services and benefit periods;
- termination and cancellation rights;
- whether amounts are accrued, prepaid, committed or already invoiced;
- whether the commitments are consistent with historic practice; and
- their treatment under working-capital, leakage and debt definitions.

Treatment should follow the verified facts and agreed price mechanics, without double counting.

### 7. Title evidence

DD-012 is only the Company’s internal share register. It is relevant evidence, but not sufficient independent proof that the Seller owns the shares free of encumbrances or has authority to transfer them.

Require customary corroboration, including:

- original or replacement share certificates;
- historical issue and transfer records and relevant board approvals;
- constitutional and corporate-authority documents;
- Seller authority and execution evidence;
- searches and confirmations regarding security interests or encumbrances;
- delivery of executed transfers; and
- Completion steps placing the Buyer on the register as owner of 100% of the shares.

ASIC/public corporate records alone generally do not establish legal ownership of shares.

### 8. Tax and IP regimes

The Seller cannot declare Tax and IP “settled” merely by putting them under the proposed general regime. These terms remain open.

We should:

- continue separate negotiation of Tax and IP warranties, covenants and any indemnities;
- ensure neither category is inadvertently governed by the general warranty cap, basket or time limit;
- resist any implication that unlimited liability has been agreed; and
- document the applicable caps, periods and exclusions expressly once resolved.

### 9. Office lease and Mossvale

On the current material:

- the office lease appears to contain a notification obligation rather than a stated consent condition; and
- the Mossvale clause appears to restrict assignment, without stating that a share sale itself requires consent.

We should verify the complete provisions and comply with any applicable notice obligation, but should not concede that either document requires consent to the share sale without a contractual basis.

## Disclosure Letter response

The Disclosure Letter contains useful factual flags but should not be accepted as presently effective against the warranties because:

1. paragraphs 1.1 and 1.2 use impermissible general disclosure;
2. several specific disclosures identify documents or uncertainty without fairly describing the consequences;
3. broad disclosure should not cure missing Completion deliverables such as Bluefen consent or Riverlark releases;
4. ambiguous statements should not disclose unknown facts or every possible consequence of an incident; and
5. the reservation of liability does not prevent a fact from being disclosed, but it also cannot expand the disclosure beyond the specific facts stated.

Require a warranty-by-warranty disclosure schedule, with supporting documents clearly cross-referenced and sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to understand each exception.

## Recommended negotiation priorities

### Must resolve before signing or Completion

1. Restore the **25% general warranty cap**, **AUD 5,000/AUD 50,000 tipping thresholds**, and **24-month period**.
2. Establish a separate **100%, six-year minimum title/fundamental regime**.
3. Insert the comprehensive fraud, wilful-concealment and deliberate-misconduct carve-out.
4. Delete broad data-room/public-record disclosure and constructive Buyer knowledge.
5. Prevent the general limitations from overriding Tax, IP, title, indemnity, payment and covenant claims.
6. Make effective Bluefen consent, with satisfied conditions, a genuine Completion condition.
7. Implement Riverlark repayment and effective security releases through the Completion funds flow.
8. Expressly allocate the AUD 420,000 bonuses and all on-costs to the Seller.
9. Verify and cure Ironquay ownership/payment issues and broaden the indemnity.
10. Obtain independent title and encumbrance evidence.

### Due-diligence and drafting follow-up

- Complete the DD-006 investigation and evidence-preservation process without assuming breach, loss or notification.
- Assess Sandbar factually rather than automatically treating it as Debt.
- Confirm the office-lease notice requirement and the scope of the Mossvale anti-assignment clause.
- Continue separate negotiation of Tax and IP protections.

**Bottom line:** the current draft is not acceptable. Its general liability structure is materially below our authorised position, and its cross-cutting limitations would weaken several protections that must remain separate and, in the case of fraud and deliberate wrongdoing, fully preserved.
